one_liner: Research copy-and-patch WebAssembly baseline JIT; OOPSLA 2021 paper: 4.9-6.5x faster compiles, 39-63% faster code than V8 Liftoff.
what_it_does: WasmNow is a one-pass baseline compiler for WebAssembly 1.0 core modules with partial WASI support, built from the PochiVM codebase to demonstrate copy-and-patch code generation. It is not a library or a runtime CLI: it ships as a Google Test executable (`main --gtest_filter=WasmCompilation.BenchmarkAll` or `WasmExecution.*`) whose tests load hard-coded modules from wasm_inputs/ (Coremark, 30 PolyBenchC kernels, AutoCAD and clang.wasm). An open 2023 pull request (#1, by titzer) that adds a main entry point loading an arbitrary file was never merged.
how_it_is_fast: Copy-and-patch: at build time clang compiles templated C++ stencil generators into object code for every variant of each opcode (how many int/float operands are already in registers, whether the result spills), and the MetaVar tool turns the relocation records into patchable 'holes' in a stencil library. At compile time WasmEmitStencil looks up the stencil for (opcode, in-register counts, spill flag), memcpys its bytes and patches a few constants and offsets, with no instruction selection or encoding, so most opcodes cost a table lookup plus a memcpy. Stencils use the GHC calling convention so the top of the Wasm operand stack stays in registers (light register allocation) and tail jumps become fallthroughs, which is why the output also beats Liftoff's code; linear memory is addressed through the x86 GS segment base inside a 4 GiB reservation.
when_to_use: Studying or reproducing copy-and-patch: a compact, working reference for building a stencil-based baseline tier for a stack bytecode.
Benchmarking a new Wasm baseline compiler against a published, peer-reviewed data point (Coremark, PolyBenchC, AutoCAD and clang.wasm on x86-64).

Running trusted, compute-only WebAssembly 1.0 modules (no SIMD, threads or newer proposals) on x86-64 Linux with AVX2 where startup latency matters more than peak speed, accepting research-grade code.
Borrowing the stencil-library build pipeline for your own JIT; the same technique was later adopted by CPython's JIT (separate catalogue entry).
when_not_to_use: Any untrusted WebAssembly: the README says outright not to, the code has had no auditing or fuzzing, the parser skips validation, and the code region is mapped read-write-execute at once.

Production embedding: there is no embedding API, no CLI for arbitrary modules, only partial WASI (other modules hit 'WASI import not implemented'), and the project has been abandoned since 2021 (4 commits).
Platforms other than x86-64 Linux: memory access uses arch_prctl(ARCH_SET_GS), the build adds -mavx2, and builds run only through the provided Docker image.

Peak-throughput workloads: it is a baseline tier only, with no optimizing tier or tier-up. The paper puts it at Wasmer Cranelift's level (2.6% slower on Coremark, 4.6% faster on PolyBenchC), below TurboFan/LLVM-class output.
Modules using post-1.0 features (SIMD, threads, reference types, multi-memory): only the 1.0 core spec is implemented.

integration.dependencies: LLVM/Clang 10.0.0 (stencil generation and PochiVM's LLVM backend are linked into the binary), Docker (Ubuntu 18.04 build image), CMake + Ninja, ccache (CMake aborts with 'ccache not found!' without it), bundled googletest
integration.thread_safety: not documented; compilation is single-threaded and the linear-memory base lives in the per-thread GS register (SetGs before running), so one running instance per thread

gotchas: Harness flaw (compile-time comparison): WasmNow's timed ParseModule never validates the module (its readers say they assume 'the module has passed validation' and the checks are assert() calls, compiled out by -DNDEBUG in the production build), while the paper times Liftoff as `new WebAssembly.Module(data)`, which per the WebAssembly JS API must validate before compiling and also builds JS objects. The paper does not mention this asymmetry, so part of the 4.9-6.5x compile-time gap may come from skipped validation rather than from copy-and-patch.

Coremark and PolyBenchC modules hold only about 30 kB of code (0.6 ms to compile, 0.2 ms of it memory-manager setup per the paper), so those ratios rest on sub-millisecond timings; the in-repo BenchmarkAll averages only 5 runs and times WasmNow alone. Neither the Liftoff JS harness nor the exact Chrome flags are published.
The code buffer is mmap'd PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE|PROT_EXEC (no W^X), and malformed input is undefined behaviour because validation is skipped.

The build sets -Weverything -Werror and requires the pinned clang 10 Docker image; a newer compiler is likely to fail on new warnings. The README says the license is MIT, but no LICENSE file appears at the repo top level.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick WasmNow over WARP or V8 Liftoff only to study or reproduce copy-and-patch on WebAssembly; to run real Wasm use a production engine or WARP, and for a maintained fast baseline back-end for your own IR look at TPDE (LLVM IR, 10-20x faster than -O0) or the CPython copy-and-patch JIT. PochiVM is the same author's sibling, applying the technique to a C++ metaprogramming AST instead of Wasm bytecode.
verified_claims_summary: OOPSLA 2021 paper (opened from the author's sillycross.github.io repository via raw.githubusercontent.com): on an Intel i7-7700HQ at 2.80 GHz (turbo on, Ubuntu 20.04, 32 GB), all compilers limited to one CPU, at least 30 runs with CI95 under 2%, copy-and-patch compiles 4.9-6.5x faster than Chrome 81's Liftoff (timed as new WebAssembly.Module after the bytes are in memory) and 12.7-18.5x faster than Wasmer 1.0 SinglePass across Coremark, PolyBenchC, AutoCAD and clang.wasm; its code runs 39% faster than Liftoff's on 10,000 Coremark iterations and 63% faster on average across the 30 PolyBenchC kernels. WasmNow was built with clang++ 10 at -O3 -mavx2.
status_note: Abandoned research prototype (4 commits, last October 2021, author says no plan to fix WASI gaps); MIT per README and readable as a reference implementation, but not for running untrusted code or embedding without substantial work.
